title: A year in Yogya — telling the story, and a proposal
title_target: Sejak itu saya merasa bukan tamu lagi
goal: Tell the story of a stretch of your life in order — first, then, after that, finally, ever since — and recognise the formal language of a family occasion. The unit closes Sarah's first year in Yogyakarta and opens a new chapter for Rina.
bekal: tell a story in sequence with *pertama-tama, mula-mula, lalu, kemudian, setelah itu, akhirnya, sejak itu*
anchor the past without tenses: *dulu, waktu itu, awalnya, sampai sekarang*
follow the ceremonial Indonesian of a *lamaran*: *maksud kedatangan kami*, *yang pertama … yang kedua*, *bersedia*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Setahun di Jogja
dialogs.intro: Pak Hendra, Sarah's old boss and now regional head, is in Yogyakarta in December for the office's end-of-year review. After the formal part, he and Sarah sit on the office terrace with a plate of *bakpia*.

notes: **Betah** has no single English equivalent: it means to be happy staying somewhere, to feel settled, not to want to leave. *Betah di sini?* is a question every newcomer hears, and *Betah sekali* is the answer that makes people smile. The opposite is *nggak betah*: restless, wanting to go.

**Awalnya, pertama-tama, mula-mula.** All three open a story. *Awalnya* ("at the start of it") is the most conversational; *pertama-tama* ("first of all") numbers a first step; *mula-mula* ("at first") sets up a contrast with what came later, which is why Sarah uses it before *Mas Bayu selalu tertawa*.

**Lapor ke Pak Harjo** — Unit 4 again. Every newcomer to a *kampung* reports to the head of the RT (*Rukun Tetangga*, the smallest unit of neighbourhood administration). The forms are real; so is the tea you are offered while you fill them in.

**Luwes** — "supple, easy, natural" — is the compliment you want for your Indonesian: not just correct, but flowing. *Katanya* (Unit 17) signals that Pak Hendra heard it from someone, probably Mas Bayu.

**Sithik-sithik** is Javanese for *sedikit-sedikit*, "a little bit". It is the modest answer to "do you speak Javanese?", and saying it in Javanese proves the point. The *th* is a Javanese sound made with the tongue against the teeth; an ordinary *t* is fine.

**Saya diajak Mas Bayu ke Klaten** — "I was invited along by Mas Bayu to Klaten". *Mengajak* is to ask someone to come with you, and Indonesian likes to tell it from the invited person's side: *Saya diajak makan*, *Saya diajak nonton*. There is no *oleh*; the doer follows the verb directly (Unit 4).

grammars.title: Putting a story in order
body: These are the signposts that turn a list of events into a story. Each has a written and a spoken form, and you will hear both in the same conversation.
after: *Lalu* and *kemudian* are interchangeable; *kemudian* is slightly more formal and more common in writing. *Terus* is what everyone says out loud, often several times in a row.

⚠️ *Akhirnya* is "finally, in the end", and often carries relief: *Akhirnya sampai!* (we've made it at last!). It is not a way of saying "lastly" in a list; for that use *terakhir* (see the second dialogue).

grammars.title: The past without a past tense
body: Indonesian verbs never change for time, so a story leans on time words instead. Set the time once, near the start, and the verbs can stay bare for the rest of the story.

head: Time word
Meaning
Example
rows: *Waktu itu saya belum bisa bahasa Jawa.*

after: Once *dulu* or *waktu itu* has set the scene, you do not repeat it: *Dulu saya tinggal di kos. Kamarnya kecil. Tetangga saya ramah.* Every sentence is understood as past.
💬 *Dulu* also means "formerly, in the old days" and can sound nostalgic: *Dulu Jogja nggak semacet ini* (Yogya didn't use to be this congested). Its partner is *sekarang*.

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Lamaran Rina
dialogs.intro: A Sunday morning later that month, in the front room of Rina's parents' house in Jakarta. Andi's family has come to ask formally for Rina's hand. Andi's uncle, Om Heru, speaks for his family; Rina's father, Pak Rahmat, answers for hers. Sarah sits at the back.

notes: **Lamaran** is the formal proposal: the man's family visits the woman's family, a spokesman states the purpose, and the woman's side gives its answer. Everyone already knows the answer; the ceremony is about the two families meeting properly. Rings are often exchanged, and the wedding date may be discussed.

**Maksud kedatangan kami** — "the purpose of our coming" — is the fixed opening of any formal visit, from a *lamaran* to a delegation at the *kelurahan*. *Bersilaturahmi* is to visit in order to keep family and social ties strong, a word you will meet at every Lebaran and every formal gathering.

**Nak Rina, putra kami.** *Nak* (from *anak*) is a warm way for elders to address a younger person, even an adult. *Putra* and *putri* are the respectful words for son and daughter; in a ceremony nobody says *anak laki-laki*.

**Bismillah, Alhamdulillah.** Rina's family is Muslim, so her answer opens with *Bismillah* ("in the name of God") and the reply is *Alhamdulillah* ("praise be to God"). These phrases are woven into everyday speech for Muslim Indonesians. As a guest of another faith you are not expected to say them, only to recognise the moment.

**Bersedia, kesediaan.** *Bersedia* is "to be willing", the formal way of saying yes to an offer or a role: *Saya bersedia menjadi pembicara*. The noun *kesediaan* (willingness) appears in every formal thank-you: *Terima kasih atas kesediaan Bapak*.

**Nyebelin** — "annoying" — is Jakarta *-in* on *sebal* (irritated): the standard word is *menyebalkan*. *Soalnya* ("the thing is") is how people really say "because" when they explain themselves. And yes: many of the best couples in Indonesian stories started with *nyebelin*.

grammars.title: Ordering points in formal speech
body: Ceremonies, meetings and speeches number their points aloud. The pattern is *yang* + ordinal, which you met in Unit 18, with a fixed set of words for moving on and closing.
after: B1 will build whole presentations on this frame. For now, notice how much politeness the frame itself carries: Om Heru never says "we want", only *maksud kedatangan kami* and *kami datang untuk*.

💬 Out of the ceremony, the same people switch straight back to *aku, nggak* and *makasih*, as Andi does two lines later. Knowing both registers, and when to change, is exactly what this book has been about.

blocks.text: Here is the kind of paragraph you can now write about your own year. Read it for the signposts: they are doing all the work of the tenses English would need.

*Setahun yang lalu saya pindah ke Yogyakarta. Awalnya semuanya terasa asing. Pertama-tama saya membeli perabot untuk rumah kontrakan saya, lalu saya lapor ke ketua RT. Mula-mula saya sering bingung, tetapi tetangga saya sangat sabar. Kemudian, waktu Lebaran, saya diajak teman ke rumah keluarganya. Sejak itu saya merasa betah. Sekarang saya sudah bisa menawar di pasar, memasak gudeg, dan sedikit berbahasa Jawa.*
A *lamaran* is the first step on a road that, in most Indonesian families, runs for months and involves everyone. Rina's wedding comes in the next book; these are the words to have ready.

rows: Sarah, I've added up this month's budget. Can we go through it together?
*Mbak Sarah, anggaran bulan ini sudah saya rekap. Bisa kita cek bersama?*
Oh, right. There were about two hundred people, weren't there?
*Oh, iya. Pesertanya kira-kira dua ratus orang, kan?*
OK. I'll get quotes from two or three caterers.
*Oke. Nanti saya minta penawaran dari dua atau tiga katering.*
Oh no, you're right. The credit's nearly gone. Where do I buy it?
*Aduh, iya, Bu. Tokennya tinggal sedikit. Belinya di mana, ya?*
No wonder. Your house is smaller, but it uses twice as much electricity as mine.
*Pantesan. Rumah Mbak lebih kecil, tapi listriknya dua kali lipat rumah saya.*
